issues.legal_issue: A party may rely on a basis for title that was not expressly pleaded when the issue was understood to be part of the trial and evidence was led on it without the other party being taken by surprise.
material_facts: The claim for possession was based on a title document in the plaintiffs’ names, and the defendant alleged that they held the property benami for its real owners.

The plaintiffs also sought to establish that they had paid the purchase price, but the parties knew during the trial that the nature and beneficial ownership of the transaction were in issue and led evidence on that question.
The defendant did not object before the High Court that the court could not consider whether the named transferees held the property for another person.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not barred from relying on the contention that the purchase, though funded by the deceased relative, was intended to benefit the second plaintiff.
issues.legal_principle: Relief is ordinarily founded on the pleadings, but a party may rely on a matter covered expressly or by implication in the issues where both parties knew it was involved and led evidence on it. The Court applied Bhagwati Prasad v. Shri Chandrainaul and distinguished Trojan and Co. Ltd. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar, where the alternative basis was not within the parties’ knowledge during trial.

rule.if: suit_involves_a_title_dispute and issue_was_understood_by_both_sides and evidence_was_led_on_the_issue and other_side_was_not_taken_by_surprise

predicates.suit_involves_a_title_dispute: The parties disputed who held title to property that was the subject of a claim for possession.
predicates.issue_was_understood_by_both_sides: Both sides understood that the nature of the transaction and beneficial ownership were in issue.
predicates.evidence_was_led_on_the_issue: Both sides presented evidence concerning the nature of the transaction and beneficial ownership.
predicates.other_side_was_not_taken_by_surprise: The party opposing the claim was not taken by surprise by the issue during the trial.

issues.definition: When a title issue was understood by both sides, evidence was led on it, and the opposing side was not surprised, the court may grant relief on that issue even if it was not expressly pleaded.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a property purchased with one person’s money in the names of others was held benami depends on the purchaser’s intention, assessed from the surrounding circumstances and the parties’ conduct.
material_facts: The property was purchased with money provided by the deceased relative, and the title document was issued in the names of the plaintiffs at his request.
The deceased relative was a bachelor, while the second plaintiff was a young child living under his care; the second plaintiff’s father was in indigent circumstances.
The deceased relative gave the original title document to the second plaintiff after he passed an examination.
Witnesses testified that the deceased relative said the house belonged to the second plaintiff and that he intended the second plaintiff to receive his property.
The defendant alleged political circumstances explained why the title document was issued in the plaintiffs’ names but did not substantiate those circumstances.
The deceased relative had no evident reason to conceal his ownership from the government that sold him the property.
issues.conclusion: The purchase was not benami; the deceased relative intended the second plaintiff to be the beneficial owner, who was entitled to possession.
issues.legal_principle: The person asserting that a transaction is benami bears the burden of proving it. Where the purchase money is provided by someone other than the named transferee, the purchase is prima facie presumed to benefit the person who supplied the money unless evidence shows otherwise; the contributor’s intention is determined from the surrounding circumstances, relationship, motives and subsequent conduct. Section 82 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, recognizes the principle that a transferee must hold property for the benefit of the person providing consideration if that person did not intend the consideration to benefit the transferee. The Court relied on Meenakshi Mills v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Manmohan Dass v. Ramdei, Mohammad Sadiq Ali Khan v. Fakhr Jahan Begum, and Jayadayal Poddar v. Bibi Hazara. It also held that the English doctrine of advancement was not in vogue in India.

predicates.benami_dispute_in_a_property_title_case: The parties to a dispute over property title disputed whether the named transferee held the property benami for another person.
predicates.purchase_money_supplied_by_someone_other: A person other than the named transferee supplied the purchase money.
predicates.named_transferee_received_title_document: The person named in the title document received or retained that document from the person who arranged the purchase.
predicates.surrounding_circumstances_show_contribut: The contributor’s statements, conduct, relationship with the named transferee, and other circumstances indicated an intention to benefit the named transferee.

issues.definition: If another person supplied the purchase money but the surrounding circumstances show that the contributor intended to benefit the named transferee, the named transferee holds beneficial title.

issues.legal_issue: A property purchaser’s later declarations against his proprietary interest may be admitted as evidence against his legal representative in a dispute over whether the property was acquired benami.
material_facts: The deceased relative supplied the purchase money and later told witnesses that the house belonged to the second plaintiff.
The declarations were made years after the purchase and were against the deceased relative’s own proprietary interest.
The defendant, who claimed through the deceased relative, disputed the evidentiary value of those declarations.
issues.conclusion: The later declarations were admissible against the deceased relative’s legal representative as admissions against proprietary interest.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 21 and 32(3) of the Indian Evidence Act, statements against a person’s proprietary interest may be admitted as evidence. The Court distinguished the rule discussed in Shephard v. Cartwright: subsequent declarations are not admissible in the maker’s favour but may be admissible against the maker or those claiming through him when they are against the maker’s interest.

predicates.benami_dispute_in_a_property_title_case: The parties disputed whether property acquired in another person’s name was held benami.
predicates.property_contributor_made_later_declarat: The person who supplied the purchase money later made a statement inconsistent with that person’s own ownership of the property.
predicates.opposing_party_claims_through_contributo: The party opposing reliance on the statement claimed an interest through the person who made it.

issues.definition: In a benami title dispute, a later statement by the purchase-money contributor against that person’s own proprietary interest may be admitted against a party claiming through the contributor.

issues.legal_issue: An occupant’s expenditure on repairs or reconstruction does not by itself confer a proprietary interest in property when the occupant knows the actual state of title.
material_facts: The defendant alleged that he had spent money on repairs and reconstruction after the title document was issued in the plaintiffs’ names.
The Court found that the defendant had not established that he spent money on the work.
The Court added that even if the defendant had spent money with knowledge of the actual state of affairs, that expenditure would not confer a proprietary interest.
issues.conclusion: The alleged repair and reconstruction expenditure did not give the defendant any proprietary interest in the property.
issues.legal_principle: Expenditure on repairs or reconstruction, even if made with knowledge of the actual state of title, does not in law confer a proprietary interest in the property.

predicates.property_title_is_disputed: The parties disputed who owned the property.
predicates.occupant_spends_on_repairs_or_reconstruc: A person occupying the property spends money on repairs or reconstruction while knowing the actual state of title.

issues.definition: When an occupant who knows the actual state of title spends money on repairs or reconstruction, that expenditure alone does not create proprietary title.

issues.legal_issue: A successful claimant to possession is entitled to mesne profits for the period of wrongful occupation, with future mesne profits determined through an inquiry.
material_facts: The second plaintiff was entitled to possession of the house, while the defendant continued to occupy it during the litigation.

The trial court had awarded damages for use and occupation, and the Supreme Court directed payment of mesne profits through the date of its judgment and an inquiry into future mesne profits until possession was delivered.
issues.conclusion: The defendant was directed to pay mesne profits for the period specified by the Court, with future mesne profits to be determined by the trial court under Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Order 20, Rule 12 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an inquiry to determine mesne profits continuing after judgment until delivery of possession. A successful claimant to possession may recover mesne profits for the wrongful occupation.

predicates.appeal_arises_from_suit_for_possession: The appeal arises from a suit seeking possession of property.
predicates.claimant_is_entitled_to_possession: The court determines that the claimant is entitled to possession of the property.
predicates.opposing_party_continues_in_occupation: The party opposing the claim remains in occupation of the property while possession is withheld.

issues.definition: When a claimant is entitled to possession in an appeal arising from a possession suit and the opposing party remains in occupation, the occupant must pay mesne profits until possession is delivered.
